text:
Rhubarb (Daio / Da Huang) — Honzō Wamyō Entry

Rhubarb [大黄, Daio / Da Huang] — Japanese vernacular name: Kawarakusa [加波良久佐]. Thermal nature: cold. Flavour: bitter. Primary therapeutic actions: dispels static [stagnant] blood [瘀血, oketsu], opens blockage of blood, treats patterns of alternating cold and heat [寒熱, kannetsu], breaks up accumulations and masses [癥瘕積聚, chōka-shakkyo], dissolves retained fluids and old undigested food [留飲宿食], flushes and purges [蕩滌, tōteki] the intestines and stomach, eliminates the old and generates the new [推陳致新], facilitates the passage of water and grain [water metabolism and digestion], regulates the middle [burner] and transforms food, and calms and harmonises the five viscera [五臓, gozō]. Preparation: the root is decocted in doses of 3–12 g; cooking time should be kept short in order to preserve the cathartic [purgative] effect. Use in Kampo [Japanese classical medicine]: the formula Daio-kanzoto [大黄甘草湯, rhubarb combined with licorice root] is employed for constipation. Contraindicated during pregnancy and in patients presenting with deficiency [weakness].

Original: 大黄 (Daio / Da Huang) — Rheum palmatum / R. officinale. Honzo Wamyo entry: 大黄、和名 加波良久佐。性寒、味苦。主下瘀血、血閉、寒熱、破癥瘕積聚、留飲宿食、蕩滌腸胃、推陳致新、通利水穀、調中化食、安和五臓。Daio, Japanese name Kawarakusa. Nature: cold. Taste: bitter. Primary uses: dispels static blood, opens blocked blood, treats alternating cold and heat, breaks up accumulations and masses, dissolves retained fluids and old food, flushes and purges the intestines and stomach, eliminates the old and generates the new, facilitates passage of water and grain, regulates the middle and transforms food, calms and harmonises the five viscera. Preparation: root decocted 3-12g; reduce cooking time to preserve cathartic effect. Kampo use: Daio-kanzoto formula (rhubarb + licorice) for constipation. Contraindicated in pregnancy and weakness.
title: Rhubarb (Daio / Da Huang) — Honzō Wamyō Entry

text:
Kanzo (Licorice Root) — Glycyrrhiza uralensis in Honzō Wamyō

Kanzo [甘草, 'sweet herb'], Japanese name Amakatsura [阿末加都良]. Flavour: sweet; temperament [qi]: neutral [平]. Indicated for cold and heat pathogenic factors [寒熱邪気] in the five viscera [五臓] and six bowels [六腑]; strengthens sinews and bones [筋骨]; builds flesh and muscle [肌肉]; multiplies strength [倍力]; treats swelling from metal wounds [金創腫, i.e. lacerations from bladed implements]; antidotes poisons [解毒]. Long-term use lightens the body [輕身] and extends the years of life [延年]. Kanzo is the most frequently employed herb across all of Kampo [Japanese classical medicine], appearing in approximately 70% of compound formulae in the role of harmoniser [調和] and moderator of the actions of other constituent herbs.

Original: 甘草 (Kanzo / Gan Cao) — Glycyrrhiza uralensis. 甘草、和名 阿末加都良。甘、平。主五臓六腑寒熱邪気、堅筋骨、長肌肉、倍力、金創腫、解毒。久服輕身延年。
title: Kanzo (Licorice Root) — Glycyrrhiza uralensis in Honzō Wamyō

text:
Keishi (Cinnamon Twig): Uses in Classical Japanese and Kampo Medicine

Keishi [桂枝, also romanized from Chinese as Gui Zhi] — the young twigs of Cinnamomum cassia. According to the Honzō Wamyō [本草和名, a classical Japanese materia medica]: 'Keishi; Japanese name, Kani. [Flavor:] pungent; [nature:] warm. Principal indications: counterflow ascent of qi [上気] with coughing and rebellious breath; constricted qi [結気] causing throat obstruction [喉痺] with difficult respiration; promotes free movement in the joints; tonifies the middle burner and augments qi.' Yoshimasu Tōdō (18th century, Kohō school of Kampo): Keishi is the foremost herb for expelling cold from the body's exterior and warming the channels and vessels. The formula Keishi-bukuryō-gan [桂枝茯苓丸] — combining cinnamon twig with Poria (hoelen fungus) — is a documented Kampo compound preparation used for pelvic inflammatory conditions and menstrual disorders, and has been the subject of multiple modern clinical trials.

Original: 桂枝 (Keishi / Gui Zhi) — Cinnamomum cassia (young twigs). Honzo Wamyo: 桂枝、和名 加爾。辛、温。主上気咳逆、結気喉痺吐吸、利関節、補中益気。Keishi, Japanese name Kani. Pungent, warm. Primary uses: descends rebellious qi, stops coughing, opens constricted qi in throat, facilitates movement in the joints, tonifies the middle and benefits qi. Yoshimasu Todo (18th c. Koho school): Keishi is the primary herb for dispelling cold from the surface and warming the channels. Keishi-bukuryo-gan formula (cinnamon + hoelen fungus): documented Kampo treatment for pelvic inflammatory conditions and menstrual disorders with multiple modern clinical trials.
title: Keishi (Cinnamon Twig): Uses in Classical Japanese and Kampo Medicine

text:
Ma Huang (Ephedra) — Honzo Wamyo Entry with Kampo Clinical Notes

Ma Huang [麻黄] — Japanese name: Umanokusa [宇末乃久佐]. Flavor: bitter; Temperament: warm. Principal indications: wind-cold [中風傷寒] with headache; warm malaria [温瘧]; promotion of sweating to expel exterior pathogens [發表出汗]; clearing of febrile heat [邪熱気]; arrest of coughing and rebellious rising qi [咳逆上気]; dispelling of alternating cold and heat [寒熱]; and breaking up of hard masses and accumulations [癥堅積聚]. Kampo clinical refinement: The physician Yoshimasu Todo observed that Japanese patients required lower doses than those prescribed in Chinese classical medical texts, and dosing was adjusted empirically over many generations of practice. The alkaloid ephedrine was first isolated from ma huang by the Japanese chemist Nagai Nagayoshi in 1885.

Original: 麻黄 (Mao / Ma Huang) — Ephedra sinica. Honzo Wamyo: 麻黄、和名 宇末乃久佐。苦、温。主中風傷寒頭痛、温瘧、發表出汗、去邪熱気、止咳逆上気、除寒熱、破癥堅積聚。Mao (Ephedra), Japanese name Umanokusa. Bitter, warm. Indicated for wind-cold with headache, warm malaria, promotes sweating to dispel exterior pathogens, clears fever-heat, stops coughing and rebellious qi, dispels alternating cold and heat, breaks up hard accumulations. Kampo clinical refinement: Yoshimasu Todo noted that Japanese patients required lower doses than Chinese classical texts specified — the dosing was refined empirically over centuries. Ephedrine isolated from ma huang by Nagai Nagayoshi 1885.
title: Ma Huang (Ephedra) — Honzo Wamyo Entry with Kampo Clinical Notes

text:
Oren (Coptis) — Properties, Uses, and Preparations

Oren [黄連; Chinese: Huang Lian] — Japanese name: Kakamikusa [加加美久佐]. Taste: bitter. Thermal quality: cold. Primary indications: heat conditions accompanied by eye pain and damage to the canthi [眥傷] with lacrimation; brightens the eyes [明目]; intestinal flux [腸澼] with abdominal pain and diarrhea; internal genital swelling and pain in women [婦人陰中腫痛]. The active compound, berberine, has demonstrated antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and blood glucose-regulating properties. The compound formula Oren-gedoku-to [黄連解毒湯; 'Coptis Detoxifying Decoction'] is widely employed in Japanese traditional medicine for inflammatory conditions. Modern clinical research indicates that berberine exhibits efficacy comparable to metformin in the management of blood glucose in Type 2 diabetes.

Original: 黄連 (Oren / Huang Lian) — Coptis japonica / C. chinensis. Honzo Wamyo: 黄連、和名 加加美久佐。苦、寒。主熱気目痛、眥傷泣出、明目、腸澼腹痛下痢、婦人陰中腫痛。Oren, Japanese name Kakamikusa. Bitter, cold. Primary: heat conditions with eye pain and lacrimation, brightens vision, intestinal flux with abdominal pain and diarrhea, women's internal swelling and pain. Active compound: berberine (ベルベリン) — antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, blood glucose regulation. Oren-gedoku-to formula: widely used in Japanese medicine for inflammatory conditions. Modern research: berberine shows clinical evidence comparable to metformin for blood glucose management in Type 2 diabetes.
title: Oren (Coptis) — Properties, Uses, and Preparations

text:
Bofu (Siler Root / Saposhnikovia divaricata) — Honzō Wamyō Entry

Bōfū [防風; Chinese: Fáng Fēng], Japanese vernacular name: Kazekusa [加是久佐, lit. 'wind-grass']. Flavour: sweet. Thermal quality: warm. Principally indicated for: major wind disease [大風] with dizziness and pain of the head; aversion to wind and wind-type pathogenic factors [悪風風邪]; blindness and inability to see [目盲無所見]; wind permeating the entire body causing pain, obstruction [痺], and fullness [煩満] of the bone joints. A prominent compound formula employing this herb is Bōfū-tsūshō-san, which remains among the most widely prescribed Kampo formulas in contemporary Japan, used clinically for obesity, metabolic syndrome, and constipation, and which has been the subject of multiple randomised controlled trials.

Original: 防風 (Bofu / Fang Feng) — Saposhnikovia divaricata. Honzo Wamyo entry documenting this as a major Kampo herb for wind-type conditions. 防風、和名 加是久佐。甘、温。主大風頭眩痛、悪風風邪、目盲無所見、風行周身骨節疼痺煩満。
title: Bofu (Siler Root / Saposhnikovia divaricata) — Honzō Wamyō Entry

text:
Shakuyaku (Peony Root) — Paeonia lactiflora in Honzō Wamyō

Shakuyaku [芍薬], Japanese vernacular name Ebisukusa [恵比須久佐]. Taste: bitter; temperament [qi nature]: neutral [平, ping]. Principal indications: pathogenic qi [邪気] causing abdominal pain; dispels blood obstruction [血痺, blood impediment/stasis]; breaks up hard accumulations [堅積]; alternating cold and heat associated with shan [疝] conglomeration [瘕, mobile or fixed abdominal masses]; stops pain; promotes urination; augments qi [益気]. — The active constituent paeoniflorin acts as a muscle relaxant, anti-spasmodic, and anti-inflammatory agent. The compound Kampo formula Shakuyaku-kanzō-tō (peony root combined with licorice root) is a well-regarded anti-spasmodic preparation, supported by randomized controlled trial [RCT] evidence for the treatment of muscle cramps and dysmenorrhea, and is among the most frequently prescribed formulas in contemporary Kampo [classical Japanese herbal] medicine.

Original: 芍薬 (Shakuyaku / Shao Yao) — Paeonia lactiflora. Honzo Wamyo: 芍薬、和名 恵比須久佐。苦、平。主邪気腹痛、除血痺、破堅積、寒熱疝瘕、止痛、利小便、益気。Shakuyaku, Japanese name Ebisukusa. Bitter, neutral. Main uses: pathogenic factor causing abdominal pain, dispels blood obstruction, breaks up hard accumulations, alternating cold and heat with shan conglomeration, stops pain, promotes urination, benefits qi. Active compound: paeoniflorin — muscle relaxant, anti-spasmodic, anti-inflammatory. Shakuyaku-kanzo-to (peony + licorice): remarkable anti-spasmodic formula, RCT evidence for muscle cramps and dysmenorrhea. One of most frequently prescribed Kampo formulas.
title: Shakuyaku (Peony Root) — Paeonia lactiflora in Honzō Wamyō

text:
Poria (Bukuryo / Fu Ling): Medicinal Fungal Sclerotium from Pine Roots

Poria [茯苓, Japanese: Bukuryo; Chinese: Fu Ling] — the sclerotium of a fungus (Poria cocos) growing on pine roots. From the Honzō Wamyō [本草和名, a Japanese materia medica]: 'Bukuryo, Japanese name Matsuhoji [末都保止, meaning "pine-holding"]. Flavor: sweet; nature: neutral [balanced, neither warming nor cooling]. Principal indications: rebellious qi [counterflow of vital energy] in the chest and ribcage; worry, anger, fright, invasion by pathogenic factors, fearfulness, and palpitations; painful binding sensation below the heart; alternating cold and heat with irritability and fullness; cough with rebellious qi [upward counterflow]; dry mouth and parched tongue; promotes urination [diuretic action].' It is widely employed in Kampo [Japanese traditional medicine] as a sedative and calming agent. Known active constituents include pachymic acid and beta-glucans, which demonstrate immunomodulating and anxiolytic properties. The compound formula Keishi-bukuryo-gan [Cinnamon Twig and Poria Pill] is among the most extensively studied Kampo preparations, with clinical evidence supporting its use in uterine fibroids and endometriosis.

Original: 茯苓 (Bukuryo / Fu Ling) — Poria cocos (sclerotium of fungus growing on pine roots). Honzo Wamyo: 茯苓、和名 末都保止。甘、平。主胸脇逆気、憂恚驚邪恐悸、心下結痛、寒熱煩満咳逆、口焦舌乾、利小便。Bukuryo, Japanese name Matsuhoji (pine-holding). Sweet, neutral. Indicated for rebellious qi in the chest and ribs, worry, anger, fright, pathogenic factors, fearfulness and palpitations, painful binding below the heart, alternating cold and heat with irritability and fullness, cough with rebellious qi, dry mouth and tongue, promotes urination. Widely used Kampo sedative-calming agent. Active: pachymic acid, beta-glucans — immune modulating, anxiolytic. Keishi-bukuryo-gan: one of most clinically studied Kampo formulas, evidence for uterine fibroids, endometriosis.
title: Poria (Bukuryo / Fu Ling): Medicinal Fungal Sclerotium from Pine Roots

text:
Saikou (Bupleurum): Properties, Indications, and Uses in Honzo Wamyo

Saikou [柴胡, Chai Hu], Japanese name Mishima [美之末]. Flavor: bitter; nature: neutral [平, balanced/temperate]. Primary indications: constricted qi [結気] in the region of the heart, abdomen, intestines, and stomach; accumulation and stagnation of food and drink [飲食積聚]; alternating cold and heat due to pathogenic qi [寒熱邪気]; eliminates the stale and promotes the new [推陳致新]. Prolonged use lightens the body, brightens the eyes, and replenishes essential vitality [益精].

Original: 柴胡、和名 美之末。苦、平。主心腹腸胃中結気、飲食積聚、寒熱邪気、推陳致新。久服輕身明目益精。
title: Saikou (Bupleurum): Properties, Indications, and Uses in Honzo Wamyo

text:
Huang Qi / Ougi (Astragalus membranaceus) — Properties, Indications, and Modern Research

Huang Qi (Ougi), Japanese vernacular name: Konomi-na [木乃美奈]. Flavor: sweet; thermal quality: mildly warm. Primary indications: carbuncles [癰] and deep abscesses [疽] with chronically festering sores [久敗瘡]; promotes drainage of pus and alleviates pain; serious wind disease [大風] and leprous conditions [癩疾]; the five types of hemorrhoids [五痔]; mouse-track fistulas [鼠瘻, i.e., scrofulous sinus tracts]; supplements vacuity [補虛]; and the full range of children's diseases [小児百病]. In modern Kampo practice, this herb is regarded as a principal immune-tonifying agent. Bioactive constituents include astragalosides and polysaccharides. Active research areas encompass immune modulation, adjunct therapy in oncology, anti-aging effects (notably telomere-related mechanisms), and cardiac protection following myocardial infarction, the last primarily attributed to astragaloside IV.

Original: 黄耆 (Ougi / Huang Qi) — Astragalus membranaceus. Honzo Wamyo: 黄耆、和名 木乃美奈。甘、微温。主癰疽久敗瘡、排膿止痛、大風癩疾、五痔鼠瘻、補虚小児百病。
title: Huang Qi / Ougi (Astragalus membranaceus) — Properties, Indications, and Modern Research

text:
Shimotsu-to (Four Substance Decoction): Formula, Components, and Clinical Commentary

Four Substance Decoction [四物湯, Japanese: Shimotsu-to; Chinese: Si Wu Tang] — One of the foundational formulas for tonifying the blood [補血] in the Kampo [Japanese traditional medicine] tradition. Formula components: Toki [当帰, Dang Gui; Angelica sinensis] 12g + Shakuyaku [芍薬, Shao Yao; Paeonia lactiflora] 12g + Senkyu [川芎, Chuan Xiong; Ligusticum chuanxiong] 8g + Jio [地黄, Di Huang; Rehmannia glutinosa] 16g. Commentary of Yoshimasu Todo on Shimotsu-to: This formula is indicated for patterns of blood deficiency [血虚], presenting clinically as pallor of the complexion, dizziness, palpitations, menstrual irregularity, and dryness of the skin. In Japan, the formula was refined with proportions differing from the original Chinese prescription, on the basis of direct clinical observation. The emphasis of the Koho [古方, 'Ancient Formula'] school upon immediate clinical observation and the modification of classical formulas is documented in Yoshimasu Todo's works Yakucho [薬徴] and Ruijuho [類聚方]. Modern pharmacological research on the individual components: Angelica sinensis (active constituent: ferulic acid) — anti-platelet aggregation activity, blood-moving properties; Rehmannia glutinosa — studied for blood sugar regulation; Ligusticum chuanxiong — vasodilatory effects under investigation.

Original: 四物湯 (Shimotsu-to / Si Wu Tang) — Four Substance Decoction. One of the foundational blood-tonifying formulas in Kampo. Components: 当帰 (Toki/Dang Gui, Angelica sinensis) 12g + 芍薬 (Shakuyaku/Shao Yao, Paeonia lactiflora) 12g + 川芎 (Senkyu/Chuan Xiong, Ligusticum chuanxiong) 8g + 地黄 (Jio/Di Huang, Rehmannia glutinosa) 16g. Yoshimasu Todo on Shimotsu-to: This formula addresses blood deficiency patterns manifesting as pale complexion, dizziness, palpitations, menstrual irregularity, and dry skin. It was refined in Japan to use different proportions than the original Chinese formula based on clinical observation. The Koho school's emphasis on direct clinical observation and formula modification is documented in Yoshimasu Todo's Yakucho and Ruijuho. Modern research on individual components: Angelica sinensis (ferulic acid) — anti-platelet, blood-moving; Rehmannia — blood sugar regulation; Ligusticum — vasodilatory effects studied.
title: Shimotsu-to (Four Substance Decoction): Formula, Components, and Clinical Commentary

text:
Hachimi-jio-gan (Eight-Ingredient Rehmannia Pill): Kampo Kidney-Tonifying Formula

Eight-Ingredient Rehmannia Pill [八味地黄丸, Hachimi-jio-gan] — A foundational Kampo [traditional Japanese medicine] formula for tonifying the kidneys [補腎]. Composition: Rehmannia [地黄, jio] 6g + Chinese Yam [山薬, Dioscorea] 3g + Cornelian Cherry fruit [山茱萸, Cornus officinalis] 3g + Poria fungus [茯苓] 3g + Water Plantain rhizome [沢瀉, Alisma] 3g + Tree Peony root bark [牡丹皮, Moutan] 3g + Cinnamon twig [桂枝] 1g + Processed Aconite root [附子, Aconitum] 1g. This formula is documented in the Ishinhō [医心方] (compiled 984 CE) as a Japanese adaptation of a classical Chinese formula. In contemporary Kampo clinical practice it is prescribed for: frequent urination, lumbar weakness [lower back debility], cold extremities, and age-related physical decline, particularly in men. It has been the subject of clinical trials addressing: overactive bladder (for which positive randomized controlled trial evidence exists), age-related cognitive decline, and diabetic neuropathy. It ranks among the most commonly prescribed Kampo formulas within Japan's national health insurance reimbursement system, with annual prescriptions numbering in the millions of defined daily doses.

Original: 八味地黄丸 (Hachimi-jio-gan) — Eight-Ingredient Rehmannia Pill. Foundational Kampo kidney-tonifying formula. Components: 地黄 (Rehmannia) 6g + 山薬 (Dioscoria) 3g + 山茱萸 (Cornus fruit) 3g + 茯苓 (Poria) 3g + 沢瀉 (Alisma) 3g + 牡丹皮 (Moutan bark) 3g + 桂枝 (Cinnamon twig) 1g + 附子 (Aconite, processed) 1g. Documented in Ishinho (984 CE) as adaptation of Chinese classical formula. Modern Kampo use: frequent urination, lower back weakness, cold extremities, age-related decline in men. Clinical trials for: overactive bladder (positive RCT evidence), age-related cognitive decline, diabetic neuropathy. One of the most frequently prescribed Kampo formulas in Japan's national health insurance system. Annual prescriptions in Japan: millions of defined daily doses.
title: Hachimi-jio-gan (Eight-Ingredient Rehmannia Pill): Kampo Kidney-Tonifying Formula

text:
Toki (Dang Gui / Japanese Angelica): Uses, Properties, and Botanical Identity

Toki [当帰, also known by the Chinese name Dang Gui]. Japanese name: Yamatorokoro [也末止己呂]. Flavor: sweet-pungent; thermal quality: warm. Principal indications: cough with rebellious qi [counterflow ascent of breath]; warm malaria [温瘧] with alternating cold and heat pervading the skin; women's uterine spotting [漏下, lit. 'dripping downward'] accompanied by infertility; all malign sores and ulcers [諸悪瘡瘍]; and wounds from metal implements [金創, i.e., cuts or punctures from bladed or metal weapons/tools]. Note: Japanese Kampo [traditional Japanese medicine] employs Angelica acutiloba rather than the Chinese Angelica sinensis — a deliberate botanical distinction developed during Japan's Edo period of relative isolation — reflecting Japanese clinical observation that the local species possessed distinct properties. Active compounds include ferulic acid, Z-ligustilide, and phthalides. The herb remains a major gynecological remedy in contemporary Kampo practice.

Original: 当帰 (Toki / Dang Gui) — Angelica acutiloba (Japanese species distinct from Chinese A. sinensis). Honzo Wamyo: 当帰、和名 也末止己呂。甘辛、温。主咳逆上気、温瘧寒熱洒洒在皮膚中、婦人漏下絶子、諸悪瘡瘍、金創。
title: Toki (Dang Gui / Japanese Angelica): Uses, Properties, and Botanical Identity

text:
Boi-ogi-to (Stephania and Astragalus Decoction): Formula Composition, Indications, and Clinical Evidence

Boi-ogi-to [防已黄耆湯, 'Stephania and Astragalus Decoction']: A compound decoction [tō] recorded in the Ishinhō [医心方, compiled 984 CE] and included in the standard Kampo [Japanese classical herbal medicine] formulary. Composition: Bōi [防已, Stephania tetrandra root] 5 g; Ōgi [黄耆, Astragalus membranaceus root] 5 g; Byakujutsu [白术, Atractylodes macrocephala or A. japonica rhizome] 3 g; Kanzō [甘草, Glycyrrhiza uralensis root, liquorice] 1.5 g; Shōkyō [生姜, Zingiber officinale, fresh ginger] 1 g; Taisō [大棗, Ziziphus jujuba fruit, jujube] 3 g. Traditional indications: spontaneous sweating [jishukan], sensation of bodily heaviness, articular swelling with particular involvement of the knees, and knee osteoarthritis. Contemporary clinical evidence: several Japanese randomised controlled trials for knee osteoarthritis have demonstrated significant reduction of symptoms. This formula is among the most thoroughly investigated Kampo prescriptions for musculoskeletal disorders. Proposed mechanism of action: tetrandrine from Stephania (an anti-inflammatory alkaloid); immunomodulatory action of Astragalus; diuretic action of Atractylodes reducing intra-articular fluid accumulation.

Original: 防已黄耆湯 (Boi-ogi-to) — Stephania and Astragalus Decoction. Documented in Ishinho (984 CE) and standard Kampo formulary. Components: 防已 (Boii/Stephania tetrandra) 5g + 黄耆 (Ougi/Astragalus) 5g + 白术 (Byakujutsu/Atractylodes) 3g + 甘草 (Kanzo/Glycyrrhiza) 1.5g + 生姜 (Shokyo/Zingiber) 1g + 大棗 (Taiso/Jujube) 3g. Traditional indications: sweating, heaviness, joint swelling particularly in the knees, knee osteoarthritis. Modern clinical evidence: multiple Japanese RCTs for knee osteoarthritis showing significant symptom reduction. One of the best-studied Kampo formulas for musculoskeletal conditions. Mechanism: stephania tetrandrine (anti-inflammatory alkaloid) + astragalus immune modulation + atractylodes diuretic effect for joint fluid accumulation.
title: Boi-ogi-to (Stephania and Astragalus Decoction): Formula Composition, Indications, and Clinical Evidence

text:
Ginseng (Ninjin / Ren Shen) — Honzo Wamyo Entry with Kampo and Pharmacological Notes

Ginseng [人参, Ninjin / Ren Shen] — Japanese name: Kurumakusa [久留万久佐]. Flavour: sweet; nature: mildly cold. Primary indications: tonifies the five viscera [五臓, i.e., heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney], calms the spirit [精神], stabilises the corporeal soul [魄, pò] and the ethereal soul [魂, hún], arrests fright and palpitations [驚悸], eliminates pathogenic [evil] qi [邪気], brightens the eyes, opens the heart, and augments wisdom and intelligence. Prolonged use lightens the body and prolongs life. Kampo [Japanese classical medicine] applications: regarded as the principal herb for supplementing qi; administered at a reduced dose compared to Chinese tradition, and combined with warming herbs in order to temper its cold nature. Active constituents: ginsenosides Rb1, Rg1, and Re — possessing adaptogenic, neuroprotective, and anti-fatigue properties. More than 3,000 modern research papers exist on this substance. Clinical evidence supports its use for fatigue, immune modulation, and cognitive function in elderly patients.

Original: 人参 (Ninjin / Ren Shen) — Panax ginseng. 人参、和名 久留万久佐。甘、微寒。主補五臓、安精神、定魂魄、止驚悸、除邪気、明目開心益智。久服軽身延年。
title: Ginseng (Ninjin / Ren Shen) — Honzo Wamyo Entry with Kampo and Pharmacological Notes

text:
Shakuyaku-kanzo-to (Peony and Licorice Decoction): Formula, Historical Basis, and Clinical Evidence

Shakuyaku-kanzo-to [芍薬甘草湯], known in English as 'Peony and Licorice Decoction,' is among the most frequently prescribed Kampo [traditional Japanese herbal medicine] formulas in contemporary Japan. It is a two-ingredient preparation composed of Shakuyaku [芍薬; Paeonia lactiflora, white peony root] at 20g and Kanzo [甘草; Glycyrrhiza uralensis or G. glabra, licorice root] at 20g. The formula is documented in the Jinkikyo [仁機経; the Japanese reading of the classical Chinese text Jin Gui Yao Lue, 'Essential Prescriptions of the Golden Cabinet'], and has been adapted within the Japanese Kampo tradition at notably higher dosages than those employed in Chinese herbal practice. Traditional therapeutic indications include muscle spasms, cramping pains, abdominal pain, and leg cramps. In modern clinical usage, the formula has been evaluated in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) for the following applications: (1) muscle cramps in patients undergoing hemodialysis, with multiple Japanese RCTs demonstrating significant reduction in cramp frequency; (2) dysmenorrhea [painful menstruation], with multiple RCTs indicating efficacy comparable to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs); (3) androgen excess associated with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), with several trials demonstrating reduction in serum testosterone levels, attributed to the anti-androgenic mechanism of paeoniflorin, an active constituent of Paeonia; and (4) chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, for which the formula is employed in Japanese oncological practice. Shakuyaku-kanzo-to is regarded as one of the Kampo formulas with the strongest evidentiary base in modern clinical medicine.

Original: 芍薬甘草湯 (Shakuyaku-kanzo-to) — Peony and Licorice Decoction. One of the most prescribed Kampo formulas in modern Japan. Components: 芍薬 (Shakuyaku/Paeonia) 20g + 甘草 (Kanzo/Glycyrrhiza) 20g. Documented in Jinkikyo (Jin Gui Yao Lue, classical Chinese), adapted in Japanese Kampo with higher doses than Chinese tradition. Traditional indications: muscle spasms, cramping, abdominal pain, leg cramps. Modern clinical applications with RCT evidence: (1) muscle cramps in hemodialysis patients — multiple Japanese RCTs showing significant reduction in cramp frequency; (2) dysmenorrhea — multiple RCTs showing comparable efficacy to NSAIDs; (3) PCOS-related androgen excess — several trials showing reduction in testosterone levels through paeoniflorin's anti-androgen mechanism; (4) chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy — used in Japanese oncology. One of the most evidence-rich Kampo formulas.
title: Shakuyaku-kanzo-to (Peony and Licorice Decoction): Formula, Historical Basis, and Clinical Evidence

text:
Sho-saiko-to (Minor Bupleurum Decoction): Classical Kampo Formula — Composition, Indications, and Pharmacovigilance

Sho-saiko-to [Small Bupleurum Decoction; Chinese: Xiao Chai Hu Tang] — Minor Bupleurum Decoction. This is a classical Kampo [Japanese traditional medicine] compound formula, documented from the earliest period of Japanese adaptation of Chinese medical tradition. Constituent ingredients and standard dosages: Saikou [柴胡, Bupleurum root] 7 g; Hange [半夏, Pinellia rhizome] 5 g; Shokyo [生姜, fresh Ginger rhizome] 4 g; Ogon [黄芩, Scutellaria root] 3 g; Ninjin [人参, Ginseng root] 3 g; Kanzo [甘草, Licorice root] 2 g; Taiso [大棗, Jujube fruit] 3 g. Traditional indications [as recognised in classical Kampo nosology]: alternating fever and chills [a 'Shao-yang stage' [少陽病] presentation], bitter taste in the mouth, dry throat, nausea, and a sensation of fullness in the chest and hypochondriac [subcostal] regions. Modern clinical applications: the formula has been extensively investigated in Japan for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B and C. Multiple large randomised controlled trials have demonstrated hepatoprotective effects, reduction in hepatitis B surface antigen [HBsAg] levels, and a measurable reduction in the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma [liver cancer] in cirrhotic patients. Proposed pharmacological mechanisms: saikosaponins [the principal active constituents of Bupleurum] modulate the NF-κB inflammatory signalling pathway; baicalin, derived from Scutellaria baicalensis [Chinese skullcap], exerts antiviral and anti-inflammatory actions. Important contraindication identified in 1994: co-administration with interferon [α-interferon, used in antiviral therapy] is contraindicated owing to the risk of severe interstitial pneumonia. The identification of this contraindication through post-marketing surveillance [pharmacovigilance] in Japan has been cited as a paradigmatic example of safety monitoring for traditional medicine products.

Original: 小柴胡湯 (Sho-saiko-to) — Minor Bupleurum Decoction. Classical Kampo formula documented from earliest Japanese adaptation of Chinese medicine. Components: 柴胡 (Saikou/Bupleurum) 7g + 半夏 (Hange/Pinellia) 5g + 生姜 (Shokyo/Ginger) 4g + 黄芩 (Ogon/Scutellaria) 3g + 人参 (Ninjin/Ginseng) 3g + 甘草 (Kanzo/Licorice) 2g + 大棗 (Taiso/Jujube) 3g. Traditional indications: alternating fever and chills, bitter taste in mouth, dry throat, nausea, chest and hypochondriac fullness. Modern applications: extensively studied in Japan for chronic hepatitis B and C — multiple large RCTs showing hepatoprotective effects, reduction of hepatitis B surface antigen levels, and reduction in liver cancer risk in cirrhotic patients. Mechanism: saikosaponins modulate NF-kB inflammatory pathway, Scutellaria baicalensis (baicalin) — antiviral and anti-inflammatory. Contraindication discovered 1994: should not be combined with interferon — severe interstitial pneumonia risk. This contraindication discovery from post-marketing surveillance in Japan is a model for traditional medicine pharmacovigilance.
title: Sho-saiko-to (Minor Bupleurum Decoction): Classical Kampo Formula — Composition, Indications, and Pharmacovigilance

text:
Kakkonto (Kudzu Combination Decoction): Formula Composition, Traditional Indications, and Modern Applications

Kakkonto [葛根湯, 'Kudzu Combination Decoction']: The most widely recognised formula [処方, shohō] in the Japanese Kampo [漢方] tradition. Composition: Kakkon [葛根, Pueraria lobata root] 8g; Mao [麻黄, Ephedra herb] 4g; Keishi [桂枝, Cinnamomum cassia twig] 3g; Shakuyaku [芍薬, Paeonia lactiflora root] 3g; Taiso [大棗, Ziziphus jujuba fruit] 4g; Shokyo [生姜, fresh Zingiber officinale rhizome] 4g; Kanzo [甘草, Glycyrrhiza uralensis root] 2g. Traditional indications [適応症]: early-stage cold or influenza presenting with rigidity of the nape of the neck and upper back, fever without perspiration, and aversion to cold [悪寒, okan]. First documented in the Ishinhō [医心方] (compiled 984 CE) and employed continuously in standard Kampo clinical practice throughout Japanese medical history. Contemporary applications: the most frequently prescribed Kampo formula for the common cold; available without prescription [over-the-counter] in Japan. Indicated during the early stage of viral infection. The constituent compound puerarin [プエラリン], derived from kudzu root [葛根], has been investigated for vasodilatory and anti-platelet properties with potential cardiovascular applications. The formula is also employed in Japanese emergency medicine settings for early-stage febrile illness. Multiple observational studies report a reduction in the duration of common cold symptoms following its administration.

Original: 葛根湯 (Kakkon-to) — Kudzu Combination Decoction. Most widely recognised Kampo formula in Japan. Components: 葛根 (Kakkon/Pueraria lobata root) 8g + 麻黄 (Mao/Ephedra) 4g + 桂枝 (Keishi/Cinnamon) 3g + 芍薬 (Shakuyaku/Peony) 3g + 大棗 (Taiso/Jujube) 4g + 生姜 (Shokyo/Ginger) 4g + 甘草 (Kanzo/Licorice) 2g. Traditional indications: early stage cold or flu with stiffness of the back of the neck and upper back, fever without sweating, aversion to cold. Documented in Ishinho (984 CE) and standard Kampo practice throughout Japanese history. Modern applications: most frequently prescribed Kampo formula for common cold. Over-the-counter availability in Japan. Active in early viral infection stage. Puerarin (from kudzu root): vasodilatory, anti-platelet effects studied for cardiovascular applications. Used in Japanese emergency medicine for early-stage fever. Multiple observational studies showing shorter duration of common cold symptoms.
title: Kakkonto (Kudzu Combination Decoction): Formula Composition, Traditional Indications, and Modern Applications

text:
Gardenia Fruit (Sanshishi / Zhi Zi) in Honzo Wamyo: Properties, Indications, and Active Compounds

Sanshishi [Mountain Gardenia Fruit; Chin. Zhi Zi], Japanese vernacular name: Kuchinashi [久知奈之]. Flavor: bitter. Thermal nature: cold. Indicated for: pathogenic qi [邪気, evil qi] in the five viscera [五内, i.e., the five organ systems]; heat qi [熱気] in the stomach; redness of the face and rosacea [酒皰皶鼻, lit. 'wine-blotch red nose,' i.e., acne rosacea]; white leprosy and red leprosy [白癩・赤癩, likely referring to distinct forms of leprous or depigmenting skin disease]; sores and ulcers [瘡瘍]. Principal use in Kampo medicine: a heat-clearing [清熱] herb for inflammatory conditions. Active constituent of pharmacological note: genipin, studied for neuroprotective effects (anti-inflammatory activity in the central nervous system), hepatoprotection, antidepressant activity (in animal models), and antidiabetic activity. Cross-traditional note: gardenia fruit is employed with essentially identical indications in both Chinese medicine and the Japanese Kampo tradition, constituting a within-East-Asian convergence signal for this drug's therapeutic profile.

Original: 山梔子 (Sanshishi / Zhi Zi) — Gardenia jasminoides fruit. Honzo Wamyo: 山梔子、和名 久知奈之。苦、寒。主五内邪気、胃中熱気、面赤酒皰皶鼻、白癩赤癩瘡瘍。
title: Gardenia Fruit (Sanshishi / Zhi Zi) in Honzo Wamyo: Properties, Indications, and Active Compounds

text:
Byakujutsu (White Atractylodes): Honzo Wamyo Entry and Kampo Clinical Notes

Byakujutsu [白术; Japanese: Byakujutsu; Chinese: Bai Zhu] — species: Atractylodes japonica (Japanese) or A. macrocephala (Chinese). Kampo medicine employs the Japanese species, representing an independent clinical tradition distinct from Chinese practice.

From the Honzo Wamyo [本草和名, 'Japanese Names for Materia Medica']: Byakujutsu; Japanese vernacular name: Okera [於介良]. Flavor: bitter. Thermal nature: warm. Primary indications: obstruction [bi 痺] due to wind, cold, and dampness with insensate or necrotic flesh [死肌]; convulsions/spasms [痙]; jaundice [疸]; arrests spontaneous sweating; eliminates [pathogenic] heat; promotes digestion and dispels food stagnation.

The Japanese Kampo preference for A. japonica over A. macrocephala emerged during the Edo period of national isolation and is attested by physicians of the Koho [古方, 'Ancient Formula'] school, who regarded the two species as possessing genuinely distinct clinical properties. Known active constituents include atractylodin and beta-eudesmol, with documented anti-inflammatory, gastroprotective, and immune-modulating activity. Byakujutsu functions as a principal digestive herb in numerous Kampo compound formulas.

Original: 白术 (Byakujutsu / Bai Zhu) — Atractylodes japonica (Japanese species) / A. macrocephala (Chinese species). Kampo uses Japanese species — distinct from Chinese use, representing independent clinical development. Honzo Wamyo: 白术、和名 於介良。苦、温。主風寒湿痺死肌、痙疸、止汗除熱、消食。Byakujutsu, Japanese name Okera. Bitter, warm. Main: wind-cold-damp obstruction with insensate flesh, spasms and jaundice, stops sweating, eliminates heat, promotes food digestion. The Japanese Kampo preference for A. japonica over A. macrocephala developed during the Edo period of isolation and is documented by Koho school physicians as reflecting genuinely different clinical properties. Active: atractylodin, beta-eudesmol — anti-inflammatory, gastroprotective, immune-modulating. Major digestive herb in Kampo formulas.
title: Byakujutsu (White Atractylodes): Honzo Wamyo Entry and Kampo Clinical Notes

text:
Ren Shen (Ginseng): Classical Shennong Bencaojing Entry with Kampo Elaboration

Ren Shen [人參, 'Man-Root']

**Chinese Name:** Rén Shēn (人參)
**Japanese Kampo Name:** Ninjin (ニンジン / 人参)
**Modern Botanical Identification:** Panax ginseng C.A.Mey. (family Araliaceae)
**Classical Category:** Superior Herb [上品, shàng pǐn] — suitable for long-term use without toxicity; nourishes life and corresponds to Heaven.

---

**Classical Text (Shennong Bencaojing, c. 200 CE):**
'Ren Shen: flavor sweet [甘], slightly cold [微寒]. It principally supplements the five viscera [五臟], quiets the essence-spirit [安精神], stabilizes the hun and po souls [定魂魄], arrests fright palpitations [止驚悸], dispels evil qi [除邪氣], brightens the eyes [明目], opens the heart [開心], and augments wisdom [益智]. Long-term ingestion lightens the body and prolongs years. Alternate names: Rén Xián [人銜, 'Man-Clasp'] and Guǐ Gài [鬼蓋, 'Ghost-Cover']. It grows in mountain valleys [生山谷].'

---

**Five Flavors [五味, Wǔ Wèi]:** Sweet [甘, gān]; some later commentators (e.g., Li Shizhen, Bencao Gangmu, 1596) add a slight bitterness [微苦, wēi kǔ].

**Four Natures [四氣, Sì Qì]:** The Shennong Bencaojing states slightly cold [微寒, wēi hán]; however, the dominant post-Tang consensus, including the Mingyi Bielu [名醫別錄] and the Kampo tradition, reclassifies it as slightly warm [微溫, wēi wēn], reflecting its qi-supplementing, yang-supporting clinical profile. Both readings are preserved in the scholarly record.

**Channel Tropism [歸經, Guī Jīng]:** Spleen [脾], Lung [肺], Heart [心], Kidney [腎] — as systematized by Jin-Yuan and later Ming-Qing physicians and adopted in Kampo formulation theory.

---

**Therapeutic Actions (Classical and Kampo Synthesis):**
1. *Powerfully supplements the original qi [大補元氣]:* The foremost herb for acute collapse of qi, profuse sweating, and devastated yang — used alone as Dú Shēn Tāng [獨參湯, 'Lone Ginseng Decoction'] in emergency presentations.
2. *Supplements the spleen and augments the lung [補脾益肺]:* Addresses fatigue, reduced appetite, loose stool, and shortness of breath due to spleen-lung qi vacuity.
3. *Generates fluids and alleviates thirst [生津止渴]:* Applied in internal heat damaging fluids, and in wasting-thirst [消渴, xiāo kě] disorders.
4. *Quiets the spirit and augments wisdom [安神益智]:* Treats palpitations, insomnia, forgetfulness, and restless spirit [心神不安].
5. *Stabilizes the hun and po souls, dispels evil qi:* In classical cosmological terms, secures the psycho-spiritual substrates housed in the liver (hun) and lung (po), and expels pathogenic influences.
6. *Brightens the eyes, lightens the body, prolongs years:* Classical longevity [養生, yǎng shēng] and adaptogenic claims consistent with Superior Herb status.

---

**Preparation Methods (Classical and Kampo):**
- *Decoction [煎湯, jiān tāng]:* Most common; typically 3–9 g dried root, simmered separately from other herbs and the decoction added at the end to preserve volatile constituents [另煎兌入].
- *Powder [散, sǎn]:* Ground and taken with warm water.
- *Pills [丸, wán]:* Incorporated into honey pills for long-term supplementation.
- *Steeped in liquor [浸酒]:* Ginseng wine for gradual tonic effect.
- *Lone Decoction [獨參湯]:* 15–30 g simmered alone for emergency qi collapse.
- *Steamed whole root [蒸製]:* Produces red ginseng [紅參, hóng shēn], considered warmer and more strongly tonifying in both Chinese and Kampo traditions.

---

**Key Classical Formulas (Kampo and TCM):**
| Formula Name | Characters | Primary Indication |
|---|---|---|
| Sijunzi Tang | 四君子湯 | Spleen-stomach qi vacuity; fatigue, poor appetite |
| Shenling Baizhu San | 參苓白朮散 | Spleen vacuity with dampness |
| Shengmai San | 生脈散 | Qi and yin vacuity with sweating and thirst |
| Renshen Yangrong Tang | 人參養榮湯 | Qi and blood dual vacuity |
| Buzhong Yiqi Tang | 補中益氣湯 | Central qi sinking; prolapse, fatigue |
| Dushen Tang | 獨參湯 | Acute qi collapse, hemorrhagic shock |
| Ren Shen Tang (Kampo) | 人參湯 | Spleen-stomach cold vacuity (≈ Lizhong Tang 理中湯) |
| Hachimijiogan (Kampo) | 八味地黃丸 | Kidney qi and yang vacuity |

*Kampo note:* In contemporary Japanese Kampo, Ninjin (人参) most often refers to Panax ginseng root and features prominently in Rikkunshito [六君子湯], Hochuekkito [補中益氣湯], and Ninjin'yoeito [人參養榮湯], among many others. Japanese practitioners generally follow the slightly warm nature classification.

---

**Alternate Classical Names:**
- 人銜 (Rén Xián) — 'Man-Clasp'
- 鬼蓋 (Guǐ Gài) — 'Ghost-Cover'
- 神草 (Shén Cǎo) — 'Divine Herb' (later appellation)
- 地精 (Dì Jīng) — 'Earth-Essence' (later appellation)

**Habitat (Classical):** Mountain valleys [生山谷]; the Shennong Bencaojing specifies Shangdang [上黨] (modern Shanxi province) as the premier source, though Manchurian (Jilin province) and Korean origins became dominant in later centuries.

Original: 人參，味甘，微寒。主補五臟，安精神，定魂魄，止驚悸，除邪氣，明目，開心益智。久服輕身延年。一名人銜，一名鬼蓋。生山谷。
title: Ren Shen (Ginseng): Classical Shennong Bencaojing Entry with Kampo Elaboration

text:
Dang Gui (當歸) — Chinese Angelica Root: Blood Tonic and Menstrual Regulator

Dang Gui [當歸; 'returning to proper order' / 'making what is due return']. 

**Chinese Name:** Dāng Guī (當歸) 
**Japanese Kampo Name:** Tōki (当帰) 
**Modern Identification:** Angelica sinensis (Oliv.) Diels — Chinese angelica root 
**Classical Category:** Middle Herb [中品, zhōng pǐn] — herbs of moderate potency used to tonify and regulate; suitable for longer-term use with attention to dosage. 

**Five Flavors [五味, wǔ wèi]:** Sweet [甘, gān] and Acrid/Pungent [辛, xīn]; some classical sources additionally note a mild Bitter [苦, kǔ] quality in the body of the root. 

**Four Natures [四氣, sì qì]:** Warm [溫, wēn]; non-toxic [無毒]. 

**Channel Tropism [歸經, guī jīng]:** Liver [肝], Heart [心], Spleen [脾]. Post-Shennong elaborations (Tang–Song dynasties onward, consolidated in Kampo practice) consistently assign primary affinity to the Liver channel, governing the Blood; secondary affinity to the Heart (which 'commands' the Blood) and Spleen (source of Blood production). 

**Therapeutic Actions (Shennong Bencaojing tradition, c. 200 CE):** 
'It governs: cough with Qi counterflow and ascending Qi [咳逆上氣]; warm malaria [溫瘧] with alternating chills and fever, with [a sensation of chills] washing over the skin [洗洗在皮膚中]; in women: uterine bleeding [漏下] and infertility / cessation of conception [絕子]; all manner of malign sores, ulcerations [諸惡瘡瘍], and metal-wound injuries [金瘡]. Administered as a decoction [煮飲之].' 
Alternate name: Gān Guī [乾歸, 'Dry Gui']. Habitat: grows in river valleys [生川谷]. 

**Subsequent Elaborations (Ben Cao Jing Ji Zhu, Tang Bencao, Bencao Gangmu; Kampo tradition):** 
Later authorities expanded and systematized the actions of Dang Gui considerably beyond the Shennong core indications: 
1. **Nourishing and Tonifying the Blood [補血, bǔ xuè]:** Principal blood tonic in Chinese and Kampo medicine; addresses Blood Deficiency [血虛] manifesting as pallor, dizziness, palpitations, and dry skin. 
2. **Invigorating and Moving the Blood [活血, huó xuè]:** Relieves Blood Stasis [血瘀]; used in dysmenorrhea, amenorrhea, and traumatic injury with pain. 
3. **Regulating Menstruation [調經, tiáo jīng]:** Core herb for all menstrual irregularities — the classical phrase 'Dang Gui is the primary herb for women's diseases' [婦科要藥] reflects centuries of practice. 
4. **Moistening the Intestines and Unblocking the Bowels [潤腸通便]:** Used in constipation due to Blood Deficiency with intestinal dryness. 
5. **Dispersing Cold and Relieving Pain [散寒止痛]:** Combined with warming herbs for cold-type abdominal pain, cold bi-syndrome [寒痹], and cold-womb infertility. 
6. **Reducing Swelling and Expelling Pus [消腫排膿]:** Addresses the Shennong indication for sores and ulcerations; used in early or unruptured abscesses. 

**Preparation:** Principally used as a decoction [湯, tāng]; also prepared as powder, wine-maceration [酒浸, jiǔ jìn — enhances Blood-moving action], honey-prepared pills, and topical poultice for skin and wound applications. The root head [歸頭] is said to arrest bleeding; the root body [歸身] to nourish Blood; the root tails [歸尾] to move Blood and disperse Stasis — a classical distinction emphasized in both Chinese and Kampo sources. 

**Key Classical Formulas:** 
- **Sì Wù Tāng [四物湯, 'Four Substances Decoction']:** The foundational Blood-tonifying formula of Chinese medicine; Dang Gui combined with Shu Di Huang [熟地黃], Bái Sháo [白芍], and Chuān Xiōng [川芎]. Kampo: Shimotsu-tō (四物湯). 
- **Dāng Guī Sháo Yào Sǎn [當歸芍藥散]:** For women's abdominal pain, edema, and Blood-fluid disharmony; canonical in Kampo gynecology as Tōki Shakuyaku San. 
- **Dāng Guī Jiān Zhōng Tāng [當歸建中湯]:** Augments the Middle Burner and nourishes Blood; post-partum deficiency. 
- **Bā Zhēn Tāng [八珍湯, 'Eight Treasure Decoction']:** Qi and Blood double tonic combining Four Substances with Four Gentleman formula. 
- **Wēn Jīng Tāng [溫經湯, 'Menses-Warming Decoction']:** Warms the Penetrating and Conception Vessels; treats cold-type menstrual disorders and infertility. Kampo: Unkei-tō (温経湯); one of the most used Kampo formulas in modern gynecology. 
- **Dāng Guī Sì Nì Tāng [當歸四逆湯]:** For cold extremities due to Blood Deficiency with cold obstructing the channels. 
- **Bǔ Zhōng Yì Qì Tāng [補中益氣湯]:** Qi-tonifying formula including Dang Gui to anchor and harmonize the Blood; Kampo: Hochuekkito (補中益氣湯), widely prescribed in modern Japan.

Original: 當歸，味甘辛，性溫，無毒。主咳逆上氣，溫瘧寒熱洗洗在皮膚中，婦人漏下絕子，諸惡瘡瘍金瘡，煮飲之。一名乾歸。生川谷。
title: Dang Gui (當歸) — Chinese Angelica Root: Blood Tonic and Menstrual Regulator

text:
Chuan Xiong (川芎): Blood-Moving Herb for Headache and Gynecological Disorders

Chuan Xiong (川芎; archaic name 芎藭, Xiōng Qióng): Flavor: acrid [xīn 辛]. Nature: warm [wēn 溫]. Channel Tropism [guī jīng 歸經]: Liver (足厥陰), Gallbladder (足少陽), and Pericardium (手厥陰) channels.

Classical Category: Recorded among the middle-grade herbs [中品, zhōng pǐn] in the Shennong Bencaojing tradition, indicating medicinal value with some caution warranted in prolonged use.

Therapeutic Actions [主治 zhǔ zhì]:
1. Invigorates the blood and moves qi [活血行氣 huó xuè xíng qì]: Treats blood stasis manifesting as irregular menstruation [月經不調], amenorrhea [經閉], dysmenorrhea [痛經], and abdominal masses [癥瘕腹痛]. Regarded as the foremost herb for gynecological blood-stasis disorders.
2. Expels wind and alleviates pain [祛風止痛 qū fēng zhǐ tòng]: Treats headache [頭痛] — particularly vertex and migraine-type headaches — and wind-cold-damp painful obstruction [風寒濕痺]. Classical texts note it 'ascends to the vertex and descends to the sea of blood,' reflecting its dual upward and downward movement.
3. Alleviates chest and hypochondriac stabbing pain [胸脅刺痛] due to qi stagnation and blood stasis.
4. Reduces swelling and pain from traumatic injury [跌撲腫痛].

Shennong Bencaojing Tradition (c.200 CE): The Bencaojing lists 芎藭 (the classical name) as treating 'central wind, entry of brain wind, headache, cold and heat [alternation], accumulations in the sinews and bones, and malign sores and scrofula-type swellings — promoting long use for lightening the body.'

Kampo (Japanese) Elaboration: Known in Japanese Kampo as センキュウ (Senkyū). Extensively employed in Kampo gynecology and neurology. Key Kampo applications include:
- Treatment of 'blood deficiency with cold' [血虛寒證] patterns, particularly in postpartum and menstrual disorders.
- Combined with Angelica sinensis [当帰, Tōki] as a foundational blood-nourishing and blood-moving pair.
- Recognized as a chief herb [君薬] or deputy herb [臣薬] in numerous classical formulas.

Key Classical Formulas [主要方剤]:
1. Sì Wù Tāng 四物湯 (Four-Substance Decoction; Kampo: Shimotsu-tō 四物湯): The primary formula for blood deficiency and blood stasis; contains Chuan Xiong, Dang Gui [当帰], Bai Shao [白芍], and Shu Di Huang [熟地黄].
2. Chuān Xiōng Chá Tiáo Sǎn 川芎茶調散 (Chuan Xiong Tea-Blended Powder): Classical formula targeting wind-cold headache, in which Chuan Xiong is the principal herb.
3. Dāng Guī Sháo Yào Sǎn 当帰芍薬散 (Toki Shakuyaku-san in Kampo): Treats gynecological blood deficiency with dampness; one of the most widely used Kampo formulas in modern clinical practice.
4. Wēn Jīng Tāng 溫經湯 (Warming the Menses Decoction; Kampo: Unkeito 温経湯): Treats cold-type menstrual irregularity and infertility.
5. Xuè Fǔ Zhú Yū Tāng 血府逐瘀湯 (Drive Out Stasis from the Mansion of Blood Decoction): Treats blood stasis in the chest and upper body.

Preparation: Typically decocted [煎服 jiān fú] at 3–10 g per dose; may also be ground into powder for external application or taken in pill form. Caution: Contraindicated in cases of yin deficiency with ascendant yang, excessive menstrual bleeding without stasis, and pregnancy (used with caution).

Original: 川芎 (Chuān Xiōng) — 芎藭 — 辛，溫。歸肝、膽、心包經。活血行氣，祛風止痛。主治頭痛，風寒濕痺，月經不調，經閉，痛經，癥瘕腹痛，胸脅刺痛，跌撲腫痛。
title: Chuan Xiong (川芎): Blood-Moving Herb for Headache and Gynecological Disorders

text:
Bai Shao (White Peony Root): Classical Materia Medica Entry

Bai Shao [White Peony Root; 白芍; pinyin: bái sháo]. Japanese Kampo name: Shakuyaku (芍薬).

Classical Category: Middle Herb [中品, zhōng pǐn] — capable of both nourishing and treating disease; suitable for extended use with care.

Five Flavors [五味, wǔ wèi]: Bitter [苦, kǔ]; in later elaborations also sour [酸, suān] — the sour quality became predominant in post-Han systematization and Kampo usage.

Four Natures [四氣, sì qì]: Slightly cold [微寒, wēi hán]; some classical sources record it as neutral/balanced [平, píng].

Channel Tropism [歸經, guī jīng]: Liver [肝, gān]; Spleen [脾, pí]; in Kampo elaboration also Lung [肺, fèi].

Therapeutic Actions (Shennong Bencaojing tradition, c.200 CE): 'It governs [pathogenic] evil qi [邪氣] causing abdominal pain; eliminates blood impediment [血痹, xuě bì]; breaks up stubborn accumulations [堅積, jiān jī]; [addresses] cold-heat [alternating patterns], mounting disorder [疝, shàn], and concretion-conglomeration [瘕, jiǎ]; relieves pain [止痛]; promotes urination [利小便]; and replenishes qi [益氣]. It grows in river valleys [生川谷].'

Expanded Classical and Kampo Actions: (1) Nourishes and regulates the Blood [養血調血] — used for blood deficiency patterns, pallor, dizziness, and menstrual irregularities; (2) Softens the Liver and alleviates pain [柔肝止痛, róu gān zhǐ tòng] — indicated for Liver constraint with hypochondriac, epigastric, or abdominal cramping pain; (3) Calms Liver Yang [平肝陽] — addresses ascending Liver Yang with headache or dizziness; (4) Preserves Yin and arrests sweating [斂陰止汗] — for spontaneous or night sweating due to yin deficiency.

Key Classical Formulas: (1) Gui Zhi Tang [桂枝湯] — Cinnamon Twig Decoction; paired with gui zhi to harmonize Ying and Wei; (2) Shao Yao Gan Cao Tang [芍藥甘草湯] — White Peony and Licorice Decoction; classical formula for acute spasmodic pain, especially of the legs and abdomen; (3) Si Wu Tang [四物湯] — Four Substances Decoction; foundational blood-nourishing formula; (4) Xiao Jian Zhong Tang [小建中湯] — Minor Construct the Middle Decoction; for deficiency cold of the middle jiao with abdominal pain; (5) Dang Gui Shao Yao San [當歸芍藥散] — Dang Gui and Peony Powder; Kampo formula prominent for gynecological blood-water disharmony.

Preparation: Dried and sliced root, typically decocted in water [煎服]. May be used raw [生用] to cool the blood, or dry-fried [炒用, chǎo yòng] to moderate its cold nature and enhance tonifying action. Dose in classical practice: approximately 6–30 g per decoction.

Modern Botanical Identification: Paeonia lactiflora Pall. (family Paeoniaceae); root of cultivated white peony. Distinct in Chinese pharmacy from Chi Shao [赤芍, Red Peony Root], which emphasizes blood-moving and heat-clearing actions over nourishment.

Cautions (classical): Contraindicated with Li Lu [藜蘆, Veratrum]; one of the classical 'eighteen antagonisms' [十八反, shí bā fǎn].

Original: 白芍 — 味苦，平。主邪氣腹痛，除血痹，破堅積，寒熱疝瘕，止痛，利小便，益氣。生川谷。
title: Bai Shao (White Peony Root): Classical Materia Medica Entry

text:
Shu Di Huang — Prepared Rehmannia Root: Blood and Yin Tonic

Shu Di Huang (熟地黃, Prepared Rehmannia Root). Flavor: sweet [gan 甘]. Nature: slightly warm [wei wen 微溫]. Channel tropism [gui jing 歸經]: Heart [xin 心], Liver [gan 肝], Kidney [shen 腎].

Primary actions: Fills and replenishes the bone marrow [tian gu sui 填骨髓]; promotes growth of muscle and flesh [zhang ji rou 長肌肉]; engenders essence and blood [sheng jing xue 生精血]; supplements the five viscera [wu zang 五臟] where there is internal damage and insufficiency [nei shang bu zu 內傷不足]; frees and regulates the blood vessels [tong xue mai 通血脈]; boosts qi and physical strength [yi qi li 益氣力]; sharpens the ears and brightens the eyes [li er mu 利耳目]. Taken over a long period, it lightens the body and arrests aging [jiu fu qing shen bu lao 久服輕身不老].

Classical category: Superior herb [shang pin 上品] in the Shennong Bencaojing tradition.

Preparation: Raw Rehmannia root (Sheng Di Huang 生地黃) is steamed repeatedly with rice wine [huang jiu 黃酒] and dried — traditionally nine cycles of steaming and sun-drying [jiu zheng jiu shai 九蒸九曬] — yielding the prepared, blackened, glutinous root known as Shu Di Huang. This processing transforms the nature from cold (raw form) to slightly warm, and shifts the primary action from cooling blood-heat toward nourishing and replenishing yin and blood.

Kampo name (Japanese): Juku Jio (熟地黄, じゅくじおう).

Therapeutic indications (classical and Kampo elaboration): (1) Yin deficiency [yin xu 陰虛] with deficiency-heat patterns: night sweats, tidal fever, afternoon fever, hot sensations in the palms and soles; (2) Blood deficiency [xue xu 血虛]: pallid or sallow complexion, palpitations, dizziness, insomnia; (3) Liver and Kidney yin deficiency: soreness and weakness of the lumbar region and knees, seminal emission, tinnitus, premature greying of hair; (4) Essence-blood insufficiency affecting reproduction: infertility, irregular menstruation, uterine bleeding; (5) Wasting-thirst disorder [xiao ke 消渴] associated with yin depletion.

Key classical formulas: Liu Wei Di Huang Wan (六味地黃丸, Six-Ingredient Rehmannia Pill) — the foundational Kampo and TCM formula for Liver-Kidney yin deficiency; Ba Wei Di Huang Wan (八味地黃丸, Eight-Ingredient Rehmannia Pill, also called Jin Gui Shen Qi Wan 金匱腎氣丸) — for Kidney yang deficiency built upon a yin-nourishing base; Si Wu Tang (四物湯, Four-Substance Decoction) — cardinal blood-nourishing formula; Zuo Gui Wan (左歸丸) — for profound Kidney yin and essence depletion; Da Bu Yin Wan (大補陰丸) — for yin deficiency with vigorous fire.

Cautions: Shu Di Huang is cloying [zi ni 滋膩] in nature and may impede digestion and the free flow of qi in the middle burner [zhong jiao 中焦]. Classical texts advise combining it with qi-moving or dampness-transforming herbs (e.g., Chen Pi 陳皮, Sha Ren 砂仁) when administered to patients with Spleen deficiency, poor appetite, or phlegm-damp constitutions. Contraindicated or used with caution in patterns of qi stagnation, phlegm accumulation, or diarrhea due to Spleen-Stomach weakness.

Original: 熟地黃 — 味甘，微溫。主填骨髓，長肌肉，生精血，補五臟內傷不足，通血脈，益氣力，利耳目。久服輕身不老。
title: Shu Di Huang — Prepared Rehmannia Root: Blood and Yin Tonic

text:
Fu Ling (Poria): Classical Materia Medica Entry — Spirit Calming, Dampness Resolving, Digestion Supporting

Fu Ling [茯苓, Poria]. Flavor: sweet [gan 甘]. Nature: neutral/balanced [ping 平].

PRIMARY ACTIONS (Shennong Bencaojing, c.200 CE): Governs [zhu 主] counterflow qi [ni qi 逆氣] in the chest and flanks; melancholy and resentment [you hui 憂恚]; fright and pathogenic influences [jing xie 驚邪]; fear and palpitations [kong ji 恐悸]; binding pain below the heart [xin xia jie tong 心下結痛]; alternating cold and heat [han re 寒熱]; vexation and fullness [fan man 煩滿]; coughing with counterflow [ke ni 咳逆]; dry mouth and parched tongue [kou jiao she gan 口焦舌乾]. Promotes urination [li xiao bian 利小便].

LONG-TERM USE: Quiets the ethereal soul [an hun 安魂], nourishes the spirit-mind [yang shen 養神], eliminates hunger, and prolongs years [yan nian 延年].

— CLASSICAL CATEGORY: Superior herb [shang pin 上品]; non-toxic; suitable for prolonged consumption.

— FIVE FLAVORS [wu wei 五味]: Sweet [gan 甘].

— FOUR NATURES [si qi 四氣]: Neutral/balanced [ping 平]; neither warming nor cooling, making it broadly applicable across constitutions.

— CHANNEL TROPISM [gui jing 歸經] (elaborated in later Bencao and Kampo traditions): Heart [xin 心], Lung [fei 肺], Spleen [pi 脾], Kidney [shen 腎] channels. Some Kampo sources additionally note the Stomach channel.

— JAPANESE KAMPO NAME: Bukuryo [茯苓]; used identically with the Chinese tradition. The Kampo tradition (derived via Tang and Song dynasty texts, formalized in Japan from the 7th century onward) places particular emphasis on Fu Ling's role in resolving dampness [qu shi 祛濕], harmonizing the middle burner [zhong jiao 中焦], and calming the spirit [an shen 安神], consistent with its classical profile.

— MODERN IDENTIFICATION: The dried sclerotium of Wolfiporia extensa (formerly Poria cocos), a polypore fungus parasitic on pine tree roots. Primary bioactive constituents include beta-glucans (pachyman), triterpenoids (pachymic acid), and ergosterol derivatives.

— PREPARATION METHODS (classical and Kampo): Dried sclerotium sliced or powdered; decocted in water [shui jian 水煎] as the standard preparation. White Poria [bai fu ling 白茯苓] (inner white portion) is most commonly used for spirit-calming and spleen-harmonizing actions. Red Poria [chi fu ling 赤茯苓] (reddish inner layer) is preferentially used for draining dampness and promoting urination. Fu Shen [茯神] (the portion growing around a pine root) is specifically favored in both Chinese and Kampo practice for cardiac palpitations, insomnia, and spirit disturbance.

— KEY CLASSICAL FORMULAS:
1. Si Jun Zi Tang [四君子湯, 'Four Gentlemen Decoction'] — flagship spleen-qi tonic; Fu Ling paired with Ren Shen, Bai Zhu, Zhi Gan Cao.
2. Wu Ling San [五苓散, 'Five-Ingredient Powder with Poria'] — for water metabolism disorders, urinary difficulty, edema; appears in Zhang Zhongjing's Shanghan Lun (c.220 CE); central Kampo formula [gohyakusan in Japanese].
3. Gui Zhi Fu Ling Wan [桂枝茯苓丸] — for blood stasis with dampness; gynecological applications; Kampo: Keishi-bukuryo-gan.
4. Ling Gui Zhu Gan Tang [苓桂朮甘湯] — for phlegm-fluid [tan yin 痰飲] with palpitations and dizziness; Kampo: Ryokei-jutsu-kanto.
5. Shen Ling Bai Zhu San [參苓白朮散] — spleen-strengthening with dampness-resolving; digestive applications.
6. Zhu Ling Tang [豬苓湯] — urinary disorders with heat and yin deficiency; Kampo: Chorei-to.
7. Ban Xia Hou Po Tang [半夏厚朴湯] — for plum-pit qi [mei he qi 梅核氣], anxiety, globus sensation; Kampo: Hange-koboku-to.

Original: 茯苓 — 味甘，平。主胸脅逆氣，憂恚，驚邪，恐悸，心下結痛，寒熱，煩滿，咳逆，口焦舌乾，利小便。久服安魂養神，不飢延年。
title: Fu Ling (Poria): Classical Materia Medica Entry — Spirit Calming, Dampness Resolving, Digestion Supporting

text:
Bai Zhu (White Atractylodes): Classical Materia Medica Entry

Bai Zhu [White Atractylodes, 白朮]

**Chinese Name:** Bái Zhú (白朮)
**Japanese Kampo Name:** Byakujutsu (ビャクジュツ / 白朮)
**Classical Category:** Superior Herb [上品, shàng pǐn] — suitable for long-term consumption; associated with nourishing life and prolonging years without toxicity.

**Five Flavors [五味, wǔ wèi]:** Bitter [苦, kǔ]; in later elaborations (post-Tao Hongjing, c. 500 CE, and through the Jin-Yuan and Kampo traditions) also Sweet [甘, gān]. The primary classical flavor is bitter, with sweetness increasingly emphasized in the Kampo tradition to underscore its tonifying action on the Spleen.

**Four Natures [四氣, sì qì]:** Warm [溫, wēn].

**Channel Tropism [歸經, guī jīng]:** Spleen [脾, pí] and Stomach [胃, wèi] channels, primary. Later Kampo and Ming-Qing elaborations additionally assign affinity to the Triple Burner [三焦, sān jiāo] in the context of fluid metabolism regulation.

**Therapeutic Actions (Shennong Bencaojing tradition, c. 200 CE):**
1. Governs [Wind-Cold-Damp Impediment [風寒濕痹, fēng hán shī bì]] — addresses painful obstruction of the sinews and joints caused by the invasion of wind, cold, and dampness.
2. [Dead flesh / necrotic muscle [死肌, sǐ jī]] — indicated for areas of insensate or atrophied musculature associated with chronic damp obstruction.
3. [Tetanic spasm / convulsion [痙, jìng]] — addresses spasmodic conditions, understood in the classical framework as resulting from damp-heat or damp-cold binding the sinews.
4. [Jaundice [疸, dǎn]] — specifically damp-type jaundice, where the Spleen's failure to transform dampness leads to pathological yellowing.
5. Stops sweating [止汗, zhǐ hàn] — consolidates the exterior by strengthening Spleen Qi and its command over the wei [defensive] layer; particularly indicated for spontaneous perspiration from Qi vacuity.
6. Eliminates heat [除熱, chú rè] — clears damp-heat accumulated in the Middle Jiao through the mechanism of drying dampness rather than direct heat-clearing.
7. Disperses food [消食, xiāo shí] — promotes digestion and resolves food stagnation by fortifying Spleen transportation and transformation functions.

**Preparation (Classical):** 'Prepared as a decocted cake [作煎餌, zuò jiān ěr]' — the classical text specifies preparation as a cooked medicinal food (a type of paste or baked preparation), suitable for prolonged use. Standard decoction (6–12 g in modern Kampo practice) is the predominant modern method. Dry-frying [炒白朮, chǎo bái zhú] enhances its Spleen-fortifying and dampness-drying properties; stir-frying with earth [土炒, tǔ chǎo] further emphasizes Spleen tropism and reduces any drying tendency.

**Prolonged Use:** 'Long-term consumption causes the body to feel light, prolongs years, and prevents hunger [久服輕身延年不饑].' This classical claim reflects the herb's classification as a Superior Herb and its role in nurturing the Spleen, the root of post-natal Qi production.

**Alternate Classical Name:** Shān Jì [山薊] — 'Mountain Thistle.' Habitat noted as mountain valleys [生山谷].

**Subsequent Kampo Elaborations:**
In the Japanese Kampo tradition, Byakujutsu (白朮) is regarded as the primary herb for 'fortifying the Spleen and drying dampness [健脾燥濕].' Kampo pharmacology distinguishes Byakujutsu from Sōjutsu (蒼朮, Atractylodes lancea / Cang Zhu), with Byakujutsu preferred when tonification of Spleen Qi is paramount, and Sōjutsu preferred when vigorous drying and dispersing of dampness takes precedence. This distinction, formalized in China by the Jin-Yuan physician Wang Haogu (c. 13th century CE), was adopted wholesale into Edo-period Kampo scholarship.

Additional Kampo-recognized actions include: calming the fetus [安胎, ān tāi] in cases of restless fetus due to Spleen Qi vacuity; and promoting urination [利水, lì shuǐ] to drain pathological accumulation of fluids in the Middle and Lower Jiao.

**Key Classical Formulas:**
- *Si Jun Zi Tang* [四君子湯] — foundational Spleen Qi tonic; Bai Zhu as principal dampness-drying constituent alongside Ren Shen, Fu Ling, and Zhi Gan Cao.
- *Liu Jun Zi Tang* [六君子湯] — extends Si Jun Zi Tang for Spleen vacuity with phlegm-dampness.
- *Bai Zhu San* [白朮散] — classical formula for gestational Spleen vacuity and threatened miscarriage.
- *Ling Gui Zhu Gan Tang* [苓桂朮甘湯] — Kampo formula for phlegm-rheum [痰飲] with Spleen Yang vacuity; one of the most frequently prescribed Kampo formulas in modern Japanese clinical practice.
- *Yu Ping Feng San* [玉屏風散] — exterior-consolidating formula for recurrent wind invasion due to Wei Qi vacuity; Bai Zhu reinforces Spleen's production of Wei Qi.
- *Fang Ji Huang Qi Tang* [防己黃耆湯] — for wind-damp painful impediment and edema with Qi vacuity; reflects the Bencaojing's primary indication of wind-cold-damp bi syndrome.

Original: 白朮，味苦，溫。主風寒濕痹，死肌，痙，疸，止汗，除熱，消食。作煎餌，久服輕身延年不饑。一名山薊，生山谷。
title: Bai Zhu (White Atractylodes): Classical Materia Medica Entry

text:
Gan Cao (Licorice Root): Classical Bencaojing and Kampo Profile

Gan Cao [Sweet Herb / Licorice Root]: Flavor sweet [gan], nature balanced/neutral [ping]. Governs cold and heat evil qi [xie qi] in the five viscera [wu zang] and six bowels [liu fu]; strengthens sinews [jin] and bones [gu]; promotes growth of flesh and muscle [ji rou]; doubles qi and physical strength; treats metal-wound swellings [jin chuang zhong, i.e., wounds from bladed weapons]; resolves toxins [jie du]. Prolonged consumption lightens the body [qing shen] and extends years [yi nian]. Grows in river valleys [chuan gu].

— JAPANESE KAMPO ELABORATION —
Japanese Kampo name: Kanzō (甘草, カンゾウ). Regarded as the quintessential 'harmonizing herb' [調和薬, chōwayaku] in Kampo tradition, Kanzō is incorporated into the majority of classical compound formulas precisely because it mediates and balances the actions of other constituent herbs, moderates harsh or toxic ingredients, and soothes the middle burner [chū-shō, 中焦]. Kampo physicians inherited and elaborated the Bencaojing designation of Gan Cao as a superior-class herb [jōhon, 上品], signifying low toxicity and suitability for prolonged use. Its detoxifying [gedoku, 解毒] and spasm-relieving [keiren-kanwa, 痙攣緩和] functions are especially emphasized in the Kampo clinical literature.

Original: 甘草 — 味甘，平。主五臟六腑寒熱邪氣，堅筋骨，長肌肉，倍氣力，金瘡腫，解毒。久服輕身益年。生川谷。
title: Gan Cao (Licorice Root): Classical Bencaojing and Kampo Profile

text:
Da Huang (大黃) — Rhubarb Root: Classical Properties and Kampo Elaboration

Da Huang [大黃, 'Great Yellow']. Flavor: bitter [ku 苦]. Nature: cold [han 寒]. Channel tropism [gui jing 歸經]: Large Intestine, Stomach, Spleen, Heart, Liver.

Classical Category [Shennong Bencaojing tradition]: Inferior herb [xia pin 下品] — potent, not for long-term use without direction.

Japanese Kampo name: Daio (大黄).

Modern botanical identification: Rheum palmatum L., Rheum tanguticum Maxim. ex Balf., or Rheum officinale Baill. (family Polygonaceae); dried rhizome and root used medicinally.

Primary classical actions [zhu zhi 主治] per Shennong Bencaojing tradition:
1. Purges downward [xia 下] static blood [yu xue 瘀血] and resolves blood obstruction [xue bi 血閉].
2. Addresses alternating sensations of cold and heat [han re 寒熱].
3. Breaks up and disperses concretions, accumulations, and gatherings [zheng jia ji ju 癥瘕積聚] — referring to fixed and mobile abdominal masses.
4. Expels retained fluids [liu yin 留飲] and stagnant undigested food [su shi 宿食].
5. Flushes and cleanses the Stomach and Intestines [dang di chang wei 蕩滌腸胃] — the classical basis for its strong purgative action.
6. 'Expels the old and ushers in the new' [tui chen zhi xin 推陳致新] — a canonical phrase indicating renewal of physiological function through elimination of pathological accumulation.
7. Promotes the free passage of water and grains [tong li shui gu 通利水穀].
8. Harmonizes the Middle [Jiao] and transforms food [tiao zhong hua shi 調中化食].
9. Pacifies and harmonizes the Five Viscera [an he wu zang 安和五臟].

Kampo elaborations (Japanese tradition, post-Tang through Edo period):
Daio is classified as a drastic purgative [gekizai 劇剤] and is considered one of the most important herbs in Kampo for conditions of excess [jitsu 実] and heat accumulation [netsu jitsu 熱実]. Later Kampo systematization (notably by Yoshimasu Todo, 1702–1773, and the Koho-ha [古方派] school) emphasized empirical formula-based usage over theoretical elaboration. Daio is regarded as indispensable in abdominal examination [fukushin 腹診]-guided prescribing, particularly where abdominal resistance and tenderness indicate interior excess.

Key classical formulas featuring Da Huang / Daio:
- Da Cheng Qi Tang [大承氣湯] (Major Order the Qi Decoction): Da Huang + Mang Xiao + Zhi Shi + Hou Po — for yangming bowel excess with severe constipation, tidal fever, delirium.
- Xiao Cheng Qi Tang [小承氣湯] (Minor Order the Qi Decoction): Da Huang + Zhi Shi + Hou Po — milder purgation for constipation with fullness.
- Tiao Wei Cheng Qi Tang [調胃承氣湯] (Regulate the Stomach and Order the Qi Decoction): Da Huang + Mang Xiao + Zhi Gan Cao — for constipation with stomach heat, less severe.
- Da Huang Mu Dan Tang [大黃牡丹湯]: Da Huang + Mu Dan Pi + Tao Ren + Mang Xiao + Dong Gua Ren — for intestinal abscess [chang yong 腸癰], appendicitis pattern.
- Tao He Cheng Qi Tang [桃核承氣湯]: Da Huang + Tao Ren + Gui Zhi + Mang Xiao + Gan Cao — for lower jiao blood stasis with heat.
- San Huang Xie Xin Tang [三黃瀉心湯] (Kampo: Sanō Shashin-tō): Da Huang + Huang Lian + Huang Qin — for heat in the chest, epistaxis, hypertension pattern (especially prominent in Kampo use).
- Fang Feng Tong Sheng San [防風通聖散] (Kampo: Bōfū Tsūshō-san): compound formula including Da Huang for obesity, constipation, skin conditions — a signature Kampo prescription.

Preparation notes: Typically decocted [jian 煎]; added near the end of decoction (brief cooking) to preserve purgative anthraquinone glycosides; longer cooking attenuates purgative action and emphasizes blood-moving effects. Prepared Da Huang [Zhi Da Huang 製大黃], wine-processed, reduces cold nature and enhances blood-invigorating action. Raw Da Huang [Sheng Da Huang 生大黃] maximizes purgation.

Contraindications (classical): Not suitable for deficiency-cold [xu han 虛寒] constitutions, pregnancy [pregnancy risk — anthraquinones, uterotonic potential], or prolonged use without monitoring.

Original: 大黃 — 味苦，寒。主下瘀血，血閉，寒熱，破癥瘕積聚，留飲宿食，蕩滌腸胃，推陳致新，通利水穀，調中化食，安和五臟。
title: Da Huang (大黃) — Rhubarb Root: Classical Properties and Kampo Elaboration

text:
Huang Lian (Coptis): Classical Chinese and Kampo Monograph

CHINESE NAME: Huáng Lián (黃連) — 'Yellow Link [rhizome]'
JAPANESE KAMPO NAME: Ōren (黄連)
CLASSICAL CATEGORY: Middle Herb [中品, zhōng pǐn] — herbs of moderate potency used therapeutically with some caution regarding prolonged use.

FIVE FLAVORS [五味, wǔ wèi]: Bitter [苦, kǔ]
FOUR NATURES [四氣, sì qì]: Cold [寒, hán]
CHANNEL TROPISM [歸經, guī jīng]: Heart [心], Liver [肝], Stomach [胃], Large Intestine [大腸] — as elaborated in post-classical materia medica and Kampo tradition.

SHENNONG BENCAOJING PASSAGE (reconstructed, c. 200 CE): 'Huang Lian: flavor bitter, [nature] cold. Governs [pathological] heat qi; eye pain; injury to the inner canthi [眥傷] with flowing tears; brightens vision [明目]; intestinal flux [腸澼, cháng pì — dysenteric conditions]; abdominal pain; downward diarrhea [下利]; and swelling and pain in women's genitalia [婦人陰中腫痛]. Long-term consumption causes one not to forget [i.e., sharpens memory/cognition]. Alternate name: Wáng Lián [王連]. Grows in river valleys [川谷].'

THERAPEUTIC ACTIONS (classical and Kampo elaboration):
1. CLEARS HEAT AND ELIMINATES FIRE [清熱瀉火]: Primary action against excess heat patterns, especially Heart and Stomach fire. Addresses high fever, irritability, restlessness, and insomnia driven by pathogenic heat.
2. DRIES DAMPNESS AND RESOLVES TOXICITY [燥濕解毒]: Effective against damp-heat conditions of the Stomach and Large Intestine, including dysentery [痢疾], gastroenteritis, and intestinal infections. The antimicrobial activity of berberine — the primary alkaloid — corresponds closely to this classical action.
3. COOLS THE BLOOD AND STOPS BLEEDING [涼血止血]: Used in heat-driven hemorrhagic conditions including hematemesis and epistaxis.
4. BRIGHTENS THE EYES [明目]: Classical use for inflammatory, heat-driven eye disorders (conjunctivitis, red and painful eyes), corroborated in both Bencaojing tradition and Kampo ophthalmological applications.
5. CALMS THE SPIRIT [安神]: Heart fire causing palpitations, insomnia, anxiety, and agitation — notably elaborated in Kampo formulas such as Ōren-dokusan (黄連解毒湯, Huáng Lián Jiě Dú Tāng).

KEY CLASSICAL FORMULAS:
- Huáng Lián Jiě Dú Tāng [黄連解毒湯 / Kampo: Ōren-gedoku-tō]: 'Coptis Decoction to Relieve Toxicity' — treats raging fire and heat-toxin in all three burners; fever, delirium, dysentery, skin lesions.
- Huáng Lián Tāng [黃連湯]: Treats disharmony between upper heat and lower cold; epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting.
- Xiè Xīn Tāng [瀉心湯 / Kampo: Shashin-tō]: 'Drain the Epigastrium Decoction' — addresses epigastric focal distention driven by heat; also used for bleeding due to heat in the blood.
- Jiāo Tài Wán [交泰丸]: Combines Huang Lian with Ròu Guì [肉桂, cinnamon bark] in a yin-yang balancing formula for Heart-Kidney disharmony with insomnia.
- Zuǒ Jīn Wán [左金丸]: Huang Lian with Wú Zhū Yú [吳茱萸] — treats Liver fire invading the Stomach; acid reflux, flank pain, bitter taste.
- Huáng Lián Ē Jiāo Tāng [黄連阿膠湯 / Kampo: Ōren-e-kyō-tō]: Nourishes yin and clears Heart fire; insomnia, irritability in deficiency-heat patterns.

PREPARATION METHODS (classical): Primarily decocted [煎, jiān] in water as part of compound formulas. Also prepared as powder [散, sǎn], pill [丸, wán], or topical wash for eye conditions. Kampo tradition notes dry-frying [炒, chǎo] to moderate cold nature when treating Spleen-deficient patients. Ginger-processed [薑製] form used to reduce nausea-inducing properties.

MODERN IDENTIFICATION: Coptis chinensis Franch. (Chinese goldthread), family Ranunculaceae. Also C. japonica (Thunb.) Makino used preferentially in Japanese Kampo. Active constituents include berberine, coptisine, palmatine, and worenine — collectively responsible for antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, hypoglycemic, and neuroprotective activities documented in modern pharmacology.

Original: 黃連，味苦，寒。主熱氣，目痛，眥傷，泣出，明目，腸澼，腹痛，下利，婦人陰中腫痛。久服令人不忘。一名王連。生川谷。
title: Huang Lian (Coptis): Classical Chinese and Kampo Monograph
